title: Against Apion 1.37-1.43 (Whiston translation)
ask_addressed: Quote the sources for how the Hebrew Bible and rabbinic texts took shape
quote: only twenty-two books, which contain the records of all the past times; which are justly believed to be divine
summary: Josephus states that the Jews have only twenty-two books held divine: five of Moses, thirteen of the prophets from Moses to Artaxerxes, and four of hymns and precepts. He does not name the books.
limits: Josephus lists a number and a division, not titles, so the identity of the 22 (versus the later 24) is inferred. Composition date from a page showing 'c. AD 97' and from Wikipedia (opened) noting Against Apion cites Antiquities, so is later than 94 CE; Josephus died c. 100. Earliest manuscript witness not established from a source I opened. Whiston's 18th-c. translation, not the Greek.

title: Josephus, Against Apion I, 37-43: Authenticity of Scripture
authors: Schiffman, L. H. (Texts and Traditions, Ktav 1998, as reproduced by CoJS)
ask_addressed: Quote the sources for how the Hebrew Bible and rabbinic texts took shape
quote: there has not been an exact succession of prophets since that time
summary: Josephus says later history (after Artaxerxes) was not held of equal authority because the exact succession of prophets had lapsed, and that no one has dared add, remove or change anything in the books. This is the closed-by-prophecy rationale for his 22.
limits: Same Josephus passage as the Whiston candidate (1.41-42), in a different translation, as printed in a teaching anthology. Josephus describes attitude and practice, not a formal act of closure. Footnote 99 on the page identifies Artaxerxes as Artaxerxes I (465 BCE).

title: 2 Esdras 14 (RSV)
ask_addressed: Quote the sources for how the Hebrew Bible and rabbinic texts took shape
quote: Make public the twenty-four books that you wrote first and let the worthy and the unworthy read them
summary: After the law is said to be burned, Ezra dictates ninety-four books in forty days; twenty-four are to be public, seventy reserved for the wise. The earliest allusion to a 24-book public collection.
limits: Pseudepigraphic apocalypse; the 24 is not enumerated here, and the identity of the seventy is debated. The book survives in eight ancient translations (Fortress introduction); I did not examine which version the RSV follows. Date from the Fortress introduction, see separate candidate.

title: 2 Esdras 14:19-22 (RSV)
ask_addressed: Quote the sources for how the Hebrew Bible and rabbinic texts took shape
quote: For thy law has been burned, and so no one knows the things which have been done or will be done by thee.
summary: The premise of the dictation: the law was lost in the Babylonian destruction, so Ezra must be inspired to rewrite it. It frames the book's account of how scripture was restored.
limits: A narrative legitimation for the author's own book (Fortress introduction: the book presumably belongs to the seventy), not a historical report of a canon event.

title: Mishnah Yadayim 3:5 (Mishnah Yomit, Kulp)
ask_addressed: Quote the sources for how the Hebrew Bible and rabbinic texts took shape; Mishnah Yadayim 3:5
quote: All the Holy Scriptures defile the hands. The Song of Songs and Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) defile the hands.
summary: The Mishnah's rule that holy scripture 'defiles the hands', followed by a dispute (Judah, Yose, Shimon) over Kohelet and the Song of Songs and Akiva's rejection of any doubt about the Song of Songs.
limits: The passage records a legal-ritual status and disagreement over two books; it contains no list of books and no act of closing a canon. Hebrew text also available via fetch_text --lang he (not quoted).

title: Bava Batra 14b (William Davidson Edition) - order of Prophets and Writings
ask_addressed: Quote the sources for how the Hebrew Bible and rabbinic texts took shape; Bava Batra 14b
quote: The order of the Writings is: Ruth and the book of Psalms, and Job and Proverbs; Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, and Lamentations
summary: A baraita ('The Sages taught') gives the order of Prophets (Joshua-Judges, Samuel-Kings, Jeremiah-Ezekiel-Isaiah, Twelve) and Writings, i.e. the same 24-book content as later canon but in a different order from the Masoretic one.
limits: Compiled in the Babylonian Talmud (3rd-6th c., Britannica via Wikipedia 'Talmud', opened); the baraita itself is undated in sources I opened. English is the Steinsaltz/Davidson elucidated translation with glosses. A list of order is not an act of closure.

title: The Redaction of the Mishnah
authors: Schiffman, L. H. (From Text to Tradition, Ktav 1991, as reproduced by CoJS)
ask_addressed: Composition dates with basis, earliest witness, and what scholars dispute (the 'Council of Jamnia' as a myth, when the canon closed)
quote: The redaction of the Mishnah by Rabbi Judah the Prince (ca. 200 C.E.) represented the end of a process
summary: Dates the final redaction of the Mishnah to ca. 200 CE as the end of a process running from Hillel/Shammai through Yavneh and Usha; Judah inherited nearly-complete tractates and an order-based classification.
limits: One scholar's synthesis; the page says it is hard to say when redaction began and that the attribution of the six orders to Akiva cannot be verified. Used as the dating basis for Mishnah candidates.

title: The Jamnia Period in Jewish History
ask_addressed: Composition dates with basis, earliest witness, and what scholars dispute (the 'Council of Jamnia' as a myth, when the canon closed)
quote: There never seems to have been a formal canonizing of any portion of the Old Testament
summary: An early dissent from Graetz's view: Ben Azzai's report does not show that the canon was fixed at Jamnia that day, the debates on Esther, Canticles and Koheleth ran on to about AD 200, and books gradually won acceptance.
limits: The DOI is printed on the Wikipedia reference to this article, not on the scanned PDF I opened; OCR text of a 1925 scan. Christie still treats Jamnia as a body of real authority and does not deny the debates, only a formal closing.

summary: Summarises the case that Graetz (1871) invented a council, that Lewis (1964) and Leiman (1976) refuted it, and that the date of canon closure is still debated, with some scholars (P. R. Davies) favouring the Hasmonean period.

title: The Canon(s) of the Jewish Scriptures (review of Lim, The Formation of the Jewish Canon, Yale UP 2013)
ask_addressed: Composition dates with basis, earliest witness, and what scholars dispute (the 'Council of Jamnia' as a myth, when the canon closed)
quote: Lim is unwilling to say that the canon was closed before the third century
summary: Reviewer's account of Lim's thesis that a diversity of 'collections of authoritative scriptures' gave way to the 22/24-book Pharisaic canon at the end of the 1st c. CE, with no closed canon asserted before the third century; also notes the Qumran community did not say what its Bible was.
limits: A review of a book I did not open; Lim's own words are not seen. The reviewer is critical of the book's method. Used to show the live scholarly range, not to settle the date of closure.

title: Masoretic Text
venue: Wikipedia (tertiary; cites Tov 1992 and M. Cohen)
ask_addressed: Composition dates with basis, earliest witness, and what scholars dispute (the 'Council of Jamnia' as a myth, when the canon closed)
summary: Reports that the Dead Sea Scrolls (c. 150 BCE - 75 CE) show no uniform Hebrew text in that period and that most Qumran fragments are closer to the Masoretic Text than to any other surviving text group; fixes the gap between the scrolls and the 9th-c. Masoretic fragments.
limits: Tertiary; the phrase is a short excerpt of a longer sentence. A reader needs Tov (1992) to check the proportions. Textual plurality is not the same question as canon list.
